title: Bengal Sati Regulation (abolition of sati)
summary: On 4 December 1829 Governor-General Lord William Bentinck and his council passed Regulation XVII, declaring the burning of widows illegal and punishable by the criminal courts in the territories under the Presidency of Fort William, and making aiding such a sacrifice culpable homicide. A secondary summary says it was extended to Madras and Bombay in 1830.

uncertainty.note: The regulation text says it was passed by the governor-general in council on the 4th December 1829.

where.historical_name: Presidency of Fort William, Bengal (governor-general in council)

importance.justification: A landmark colonial-era law criminalising sati, widely treated as an early social-reform measure in India.

audience_note: Concerns the practice of burning widows on their husbands’ funeral pyres, described in the source regulation as a crime against human life.

sources.title: Sati: Official Documents, Lord William Cavendish Bentinck
sources.publisher: Center for History and New Media, George Mason University

sources.title: Abolition of Sati and Social Reform

reviewer_note: Pinned at Kolkata as the seat of the governor-general in council; the sources name the Presidency of Fort William, not a city. The 1830 extension to Madras and Bombay is from GKToday only. GKToday is an exam-prep site; the regulation text is from the GMU page.
